title: The Spread of Agriculture in Prehistoric Europe
subject: anthro
paras: Farming did not begin in Europe. The domestication of wheat, barley, sheep, and goats first took place in the Fertile Crescent of Southwest Asia around 11,000 years ago. Over the following four thousand years, agriculture gradually appeared across Europe, reaching the British Isles and Scandinavia by about 6,000 years ago. For much of the twentieth century, archaeologists debated how this transition happened: did farming spread because farmers themselves migrated into Europe, or because local hunter-gatherers adopted new crops and animals from their neighbors?

The first explanation, often called demic diffusion, holds that growing farming populations expanded steadily outward, replacing or absorbing the hunting groups they met. Agriculture can support far more people per square kilometer than hunting and gathering, so farming communities would have had larger families and a constant need for new land. A well-known model proposed in the 1970s calculated that a slow expansion of about one kilometer per year would be enough to explain the arrival times of farming across the continent.

The second explanation, cultural diffusion, emphasizes the role of the native population. In this view, ideas, seeds, and livestock passed from group to group through trade and marriage, while the people themselves largely stayed in place. Supporters pointed to regions such as the Baltic coast, where hunter-gatherers continued to fish and hunt for centuries while also making pottery and keeping a few domestic animals. These mixed economies suggested that adoption could be partial and selective rather than sudden.

For decades, the evidence available to archaeologists, mainly tools, pottery styles, and plant remains, could be interpreted in favor of either theory. A new type of evidence has since changed the debate. Ancient DNA extracted from skeletons shows that the earliest farmers in central Europe were genetically very different from the hunter-gatherers who lived there before them and were closely related to populations in Anatolia, in present-day Turkey. This strongly suggests that large-scale migration did take place.

The genetic record does not, however, show simple replacement. Over time, the proportion of hunter-gatherer ancestry in farming communities increased, indicating that the two groups mixed, sometimes many centuries after first contact. In some northern and western regions, local foragers seem to have taken up farming themselves. Most researchers now accept that both processes operated, with migration dominant in some areas and cultural exchange in others. The spread of agriculture, in other words, was not a single event but a patchwork of local histories.
